old: "Young man," he continued, raising his head, "I seem to read some kind of trouble in your face. I noticed it the moment you walked in, and that's why I spoke to you. Because in sharing the story of my life, I don't want to make myself a laughingstock before these idle listeners who know it all already -- I'm looking for a person of feeling and education. Know then that my wife was educated at a prestigious school for noble girls, and upon graduating she performed the shawl dance before the governor and other dignitaries, for which she received a gold medal and a certificate of merit. The medal... well, the medal was sold long ago, hmm... but the certificate is still in her trunk, and not long ago she showed it to our landlady. Even though she's almost always fighting with the landlady, she wanted someone to know about her past honors and happier days. I don't blame her for it, not at all, because the only thing she has left is memories -- everything else has turned to dust and ashes. Yes, yes, she's a proud woman, spirited and determined. She scrubs floors herself and eats nothing but black bread, but she will not tolerate disrespect. That's why she wouldn't stand for Mr. Lebeziatnikov's rudeness, and when he beat her for it, she took to her bed more from the wound to her pride than from the blows. She was a widow when I married her, with three children, each smaller than the last. She had married her first husband, an infantry officer, for love and eloped with him from her father's house. She adored her husband, but he took to cards, got into trouble, and died. He beat her near the end -- though she gave as good as she got, as I have documented proof -- and to this day she speaks of him through tears and throws him in my face. And I'm glad, I'm glad that even if only in her imagination, she can think of herself as having once been happy.... She was left with three children in a remote, godforsaken district where I happened to be at the time, and in such hopeless poverty that, though I've seen my share of hardship, I can't begin to describe it. Her relatives had all abandoned her. And she was proud, fiercely proud.... And then, honored sir, I, a widower at the time with a fourteen-year-old daughter from my first marriage, offered her my hand, because I couldn't bear to see such suffering. You can judge the depth of her desperation -- that she, an educated, cultured woman from a distinguished family, agreed to marry me. But she did! Weeping and wringing her hands, she married me! Because she had absolutely nowhere to turn. Do you understand, sir, do you understand what it means to have absolutely nowhere to turn? No, you don't understand that yet.... For a whole year I did my duty faithfully and never touched this" -- he tapped the jug with his finger -- "because I have feelings. But even so, I couldn't please her. And then I lost my position too, through no fault of my own but due to staff changes, and that's when I did touch it!... It will be a year and a half now since we finally landed in this magnificent capital, adorned with countless monuments, after many wanderings and disasters. Here I found a position.... I found it and lost it again. Do you follow? This time it was my own fault -- my weakness got the better of me.... We now rent part of a room from Amalia Fyodorovna Lippewechsel, and what we live on and how we pay our rent, I couldn't tell you. There are many other people living there besides us. It's chaos, absolute bedlam... hmm... yes... And meanwhile my daughter from my first marriage has grown up. What she had to endure from her stepmother while growing up, I won't speak of. Katerina Ivanovna may be full of generous feelings, but she's a spirited woman, irritable and short-tempered.... But there's no use going into that! Sonya, as you can imagine, received no education. I tried four years ago to teach her some geography and world history, but since I wasn't exactly an expert myself and we had no proper textbooks -- and whatever books we had... hmm, well, we don't even have those now -- so all her education came to an end. We stopped at Cyrus of Persia. Since she's come of age, she's read some romantic novels, and recently she read a book she got through Mr. Lebeziatnikov -- Lewes's Physiology -- have you heard of it? -- and even told us about parts of it. That's the entirety of her education. And now, honored sir, I'd like to ask you a private question. How much do you think a decent, impoverished girl can earn through honest work? She can't make fifteen kopecks a day if she's respectable and has no special talent, not even working without pause! And on top of that, Ivan Ivanovich Klopstock, the civil counselor -- have you heard of him? -- still hasn't paid her for the half-dozen linen shirts she made him, and drove her away with shouting and insults, claiming the collars weren't sewn right and were crooked. And the little ones are going hungry.... And Katerina Ivanovna paces the room wringing her hands, with her cheeks flushed red the way they always are with that disease. 'Here you are living with us,' she says, 'eating and drinking and staying warm, and what do you contribute?' As if there's much to eat and drink when the children haven't seen a crust in three days! I was lying there at the time... well, so what! I was lying there drunk, and I heard my Sonya answer -- she has a gentle spirit, a soft little voice... fair hair, such a pale, thin little face -- she said: 'Katerina Ivanovna, am I really supposed to do something like that?' Now, Darya Frantsovna, a woman of evil reputation well known to the police, had tried two or three times to get to Sonya through the landlady. 'And why not?' Katerina Ivanovna sneered. 'What are you, some kind of treasure that needs protecting?' But don't blame her, don't blame her, honored sir! She wasn't herself when she said it -- she was out of her mind with illness and the children crying from hunger. And she said it more to wound than anything else.... That's Katerina Ivanovna's nature -- when children cry, even from hunger, she starts hitting them. At six o'clock I watched Sonya get up, put on her headscarf and her cape, and leave the apartment. Around nine she came back. She walked straight up to Katerina Ivanovna and laid thirty rubles on the table in front of her, in silence. Not a word, not even a glance -- she just picked up our big green _drap de dames_ shawl, covered her head and face with it, and lay down on the bed facing the wall. Only her small shoulders and body kept shuddering.... And I lay there, same as before.... And then I saw, young man, I saw Katerina Ivanovna, in the same silence, go over to Sonya's little bed. She knelt there all evening, kissing Sonya's feet, and would not get up. And then they both fell asleep in each other's arms... together... yes... and I... lay there drunk."

old: "Since then, sir," he continued after a brief pause, "since then, owing to an unfortunate incident and information supplied by malicious people -- in which Darya Frantsovna played a leading role, claiming she had been treated disrespectfully -- since then my daughter Sofya Semyonovna has been required to carry a yellow ticket, and because of that she can no longer live with us. Our landlady, Amalia Fyodorovna, wouldn't allow it -- though she herself had been in league with Darya Frantsovna before -- and Mr. Lebeziatnikov too... hmm.... All the trouble between him and Katerina Ivanovna was because of Sonya. At first he had tried to court Sonya himself, but then suddenly got on his high horse: 'How,' he said, 'can a man of my education live under the same roof as a girl like that?' And Katerina Ivanovna stood up for her, wouldn't let it go... and that's how things ended up. Sonya visits us now, mostly after dark. She comforts Katerina Ivanovna and gives her everything she can.... She has a room at the Kapernaumovs' -- they're tailors. Kapernaumov is a lame man with a cleft palate, and his entire large family has cleft palates too. His wife as well. They all live in one room, but Sonya has her own, partitioned off.... Hmm... yes... very poor people, all with cleft palates... yes. So I got up the next morning, put on my rags, raised my hands to heaven, and went to see his excellency Ivan Afanasyevich. Do you know his excellency Ivan Afanasyevich? No? Then you don't know a man of God. He is wax... wax before the face of the Lord, even as wax melts!... His eyes were moist when he heard my story. 'Marmeladov, once already you have disappointed my expectations... I'll take you back one more time, on my own responsibility,' he said. 'Remember that,' he said. 'Now you may go.' I kissed the dust at his feet -- in my thoughts only, because in reality he would never have allowed it, being a statesman and a man of modern, progressive, enlightened views. I went home, and when I announced that I'd been taken back into service and would be receiving a salary again -- my God, what a celebration there was!..."

old: "That was five weeks ago, sir. Yes.... As soon as Katerina Ivanovna and Sonya heard the news -- Lord have mercy, it was as if I'd entered the kingdom of heaven. Before, I could lie around like an animal and get nothing but abuse. Now they were tiptoeing around, shushing the children: 'Semyon Zakharovich is tired from his work at the office, he's resting -- shh!' They made me coffee before work and heated real cream for me! Real cream, do you hear? And how they scraped together the money for a decent set of clothes -- eleven rubles and fifty kopecks -- I can't imagine. Boots, cotton shirt fronts, a uniform -- magnificent, all of it, for eleven and a half rubles. The first morning I came home from the office, Katerina Ivanovna had cooked a two-course dinner: soup and salted beef with horseradish. We'd never dreamed of anything like it. She didn't own any dresses, not a single one, but she made herself up as if she were going visiting -- and with nothing to work with, she managed to look quite presentable. She'd done her hair nicely, put on some kind of clean collar and cuffs, and there she was, a completely different person -- younger, prettier. Sonya, my darling, had only helped with money: 'For the time being,' she said, 'it's better if I don't visit too often. Maybe after dark, when no one can see.' Do you hear that? I lay down for a nap after dinner, and would you believe it -- even though Katerina Ivanovna had quarreled bitterly with our landlady Amalia Fyodorovna just a week before, she couldn't resist inviting her in for coffee. For two hours they sat there whispering. 'Semyon Zakharovich is back in service now, drawing a salary,' she told her, 'and he went to see his excellency in person, and his excellency himself came out to meet him, made everyone else wait, and led Semyon Zakharovich by the hand into his private office.' Do you hear? 'Of course,' he said, 'Semyon Zakharovich, remembering your past services,' he said, 'and despite your unfortunate weakness, since you now give your word and since we've managed poorly without you' -- do you hear? -- 'I am relying on your word as a gentleman.' And all of that, let me tell you, she made up herself, and not just to show off -- no, she actually believes it, she entertains herself with her own fantasies, I swear she does! And I don't blame her, I don't!... Six days ago, when I brought home my first full paycheck -- twenty-three rubles and forty kopecks -- she called me her darling. 'Darling,' she said, 'my little darling.' And when we were alone, you understand? You wouldn't exactly call me a handsome man, and I'm hardly an ideal husband, would you?... Well, she pinched my cheek and said, 'My little darling.'"

old: "Why feel sorry for me, you ask? Yes! There's nothing to feel sorry about! I should be crucified, crucified on a cross, not pitied! Crucify me, judge, crucify me -- but pity me while you do it! And then I'll go to be crucified of my own free will, because it's not pleasure I'm after but tears and suffering!... Do you think, you who sell drink, that this bottle has been sweet to me? It was suffering I sought at the bottom of it, tears and suffering, and I found them, I tasted them. But He will have pity on us -- He who had pity on all mankind, who understood every person and everything. He is the One, He is the judge. He will come on that day and He will ask: 'Where is the daughter who sacrificed herself for her sick, consumptive stepmother and for the small children of another? Where is the daughter who had pity on the wretched drunkard, her earthly father, undaunted by his degradation?' And He will say: 'Come to me! I have already forgiven you once.... I have forgiven you once.... Your sins, which are many, are forgiven, for you have loved much....' And He will forgive my Sonya -- He will forgive her, I know it... I felt it in my heart when I was with her just now! And He will judge and forgive everyone -- the good and the wicked, the wise and the humble.... And when He has finished with all of them, He will call out to us: 'You, too, come forward!' He will say. 'Come forward, you drunkards! Come forward, you weaklings! Come forward, you children of shame!' And we will all come forward, without shame, and we will stand before Him. And He will say: 'You are swine, made in the image of the Beast and bearing his mark. But come, even you!' And the wise ones and the clever ones will say: 'Lord, why do you receive these people?' And He will say: 'I receive them, oh wise ones, I receive them, oh clever ones, because not one of them ever believed himself worthy of this.' And He will stretch out His hands to us, and we will fall down before Him... and we will weep... and we will understand everything! Then we will understand everything!... And everyone will understand -- Katerina Ivanovna, too... she will understand.... Lord, Thy kingdom come!" And he collapsed onto the bench, exhausted and helpless, looking at no one, lost in deep thought. His words had made a certain impression. There was a moment of silence, but then the laughter and cursing started up again.

old: "It's not Katerina Ivanovna I'm afraid of now," he muttered anxiously, "and not that she'll start pulling my hair. Who cares about my hair! Forget my hair! That's what I say! It's actually better if she does pull it -- that's not what scares me... it's her eyes I'm afraid of... yes, her eyes... the redness in her cheeks frightens me too... and the way she breathes.... Have you noticed how people with that disease breathe when they're worked up? I'm scared of the children crying, too.... Because if Sonya hasn't brought them food... I don't know what's happened! I don't know! But the blows I'm not afraid of.... Know this, sir: those blows are not painful to me -- they're actually a pleasure. I can't do without them, in fact.... It's better this way. Let her hit me -- it eases her heart... it's better.... There's the building. Kozel's building, the cabinetmaker's. A German, well-off. Lead the way!"

old: A grimy little door at the very top of the staircase stood ajar. A feeble candle stub lit up a very poor room about ten paces long, all of it visible from the doorway. Everything was in disarray, littered with rags of every kind, mostly children's clothes. A tattered sheet was strung across the far corner -- behind it was probably the bed. The room contained nothing but two chairs and a sofa upholstered in American leather, full of holes, in front of which stood a plain, unpainted, uncovered kitchen table. A sputtering tallow candle in an iron holder stood on the edge of the table. The family apparently had a room to themselves rather than a partitioned space, but their room was essentially a hallway. The door to the other rooms -- or rather the closet-sized compartments into which Amalia Lippewechsel's apartment was divided -- stood half open, and from behind it came shouting, uproar, and laughter. old: The young man hurried toward the door without a word. The inner door had swung wide open, and curious faces were peering through it. Coarse, laughing faces with pipes and cigarettes, heads wearing caps, crowded the doorway. Further back you could see figures in open dressing gowns and various states of undress, some holding cards. They were especially entertained when Marmeladov, being dragged around by his hair, shouted that it was a comfort to him. Some even started filing into the room. Finally a harsh, shrill screech rang out -- it was Amalia Lippewechsel herself, pushing her way through the crowd, trying to restore order in her own fashion, threatening the poor woman for the hundredth time with eviction the next day. As he left, Raskolnikov managed to reach into his pocket, grab the copper coins he had gotten as change for his ruble in the tavern, and set them on the windowsill unnoticed. Then, on the stairs, he changed his mind and nearly went back.

old: "What a stupid thing I've done," he thought. "They have Sonya, and I need the money myself." But realizing it would be impossible to take it back now, and that he wouldn't have taken it back anyway, he shrugged it off and headed to his lodgings. "Sonya needs pomade too," he said as he walked, laughing bitterly. "This kind of smartness costs money.... Hmm! And maybe Sonya herself will go bankrupt today, because there's always a risk in it -- hunting big game, panning for gold.... Then they'd all be without a crust tomorrow if it weren't for my money. Good for Sonya! What a gold mine they've dug there! And they're certainly making the most of it! Oh yes, they are! They've cried about it and gotten used to it. People get used to anything, the scoundrels!"

old: "My dear Rodya," his mother wrote. "It's been two months since I last wrote to you, and that has caused me pain and even kept me awake at night. But I'm sure you won't blame me for the silence -- it couldn't be helped. You know how much I love you. You are everything to Dunya and me -- our only hope, our only anchor. What grief it was for me to learn that you had left the university some months ago because you couldn't support yourself, and that you had lost your tutoring work and other income! How could I help you on my hundred-and-twenty-ruble pension? The fifteen rubles I sent you four months ago were borrowed, as you know, against my pension from Vasily Ivanovich Vakhrushin, a merchant here in town. He's a kindhearted man and was a friend of your father's. But having given him the right to collect my pension, I had to wait until the debt was repaid, which has only just happened. That's why I haven't been able to send you anything. But now, thank God, I believe I can send you more, and in fact we have reason to congratulate ourselves on a piece of good fortune, which I hasten to tell you about. First -- would you believe it, dear Rodya -- your sister has been living with me these last six weeks, and we won't be separated again. Thank God, her suffering is over. But let me tell you everything in order, so you know exactly what happened and everything we've been hiding from you. When you wrote two months ago that you'd heard Dunya was having a hard time at the Svidrigailovs', and asked me for details -- what could I have written? If I'd told you the whole truth, you would have dropped everything and come to us, even on foot -- I know your character and your feelings, and you would never stand for your sister being mistreated. I was desperate myself, but what could I do? Besides, I didn't know the full truth then. The biggest problem was that Dunya had received a hundred rubles in advance when she took the governess position, on condition that it would be deducted from her monthly salary. So she couldn't leave without repaying the debt. That sum -- now I can explain everything, my precious Rodya -- she had taken mainly to send you the sixty rubles you so desperately needed, which you received from us last year. We lied to you then, saying the money came from Dunya's savings, but it wasn't so. Now I'm telling you the truth because, thank God, things have changed for the better, and so you can see how much Dunya loves you and what kind of heart she has. At first, indeed, Mr. Svidrigailov treated her very rudely, making disrespectful and mocking remarks at the table.... But I don't want to go into all those painful details, since it's all over now. In short, despite the kind and generous behavior of Marfa Petrovna -- Mr. Svidrigailov's wife -- and the rest of the household, Dunya had a very hard time, especially when Mr. Svidrigailov, reverting to his old regimental habits, had been drinking. And how do you think it all turned out? Would you believe that this ridiculous man had been in love with Dunya from the very beginning but had hidden it behind rudeness and contempt? Perhaps he was ashamed of his own hopeless desires, horrified by himself, considering his age and the fact that he was a family man -- and that made him angry at Dunya. Or perhaps he hoped that his rude, sneering behavior would hide the truth from everyone else. But in the end he lost all self-control and had the audacity to make Dunya an open and shameless proposal, promising her all kinds of things, offering to abandon everything and take her to another estate or even abroad. You can imagine what she went through! She couldn't leave at once, not only because of the debt but also to spare Marfa Petrovna's feelings, since suspicions would have been aroused and Dunya would have been blamed for causing a family rift. It would have meant a terrible scandal for Dunya, too -- that was unavoidable. There were other reasons as well that made it impossible for Dunya to escape that awful house for another six weeks. You know Dunya -- you know how smart she is, how strong her will is. She can endure a great deal and even in the most desperate circumstances manages to stay resolute. She didn't even write to me about everything, for fear of upsetting me, though we wrote to each other constantly. It all ended very unexpectedly. Marfa Petrovna accidentally overheard her husband begging Dunya in the garden, and, putting entirely the wrong interpretation on the scene, blamed Dunya for everything. A terrible scene broke out between them right there in the garden. Marfa Petrovna went so far as to hit Dunya, refused to listen to a word, and screamed at her for a solid hour. Then she ordered Dunya packed off to me immediately in a peasant cart, into which they threw all her belongings -- clothes, linens, everything -- in a heap, without folding or packing any of it. And then a heavy rainstorm broke out, and Dunya, humiliated and shamed, had to ride with a peasant in an open cart for all seventeen versts into town. Now imagine what I could have written to you two months ago in response to your letter. I was in despair. I didn't dare write you the truth because you would have been miserable, outraged, and furious -- and what could you have done? You could only have ruined yourself, and Dunya wouldn't have allowed it. Yet how could I fill my letter with trivialities when my heart was so full of grief? For a whole month the town was buzzing with this scandal, and it reached the point where Dunya and I didn't dare go to church because of the contemptuous looks, the whispers, and even the remarks said aloud about us. All our acquaintances avoided us, no one would even greet us in the street, and I heard that some shop clerks were planning to humiliate us by smearing our gates with tar, so that the landlord started telling us we'd have to move. All of this was Marfa Petrovna's doing -- she managed to slander Dunya and drag her name through the mud in every household. She knows everyone in the area, and that whole month she kept coming into town. Being rather talkative and fond of airing her family grievances -- which isn't right -- she spread her version of events not just through the town but across the entire district. It made me ill, but Dunya bore it better than I did. If you could have seen how she endured it all, comforting and cheering me! She's an angel! But by God's mercy, our suffering was cut short. Mr. Svidrigailov came to his senses, repented, and -- probably feeling sorry for Dunya -- presented Marfa Petrovna with complete and undeniable proof of Dunya's innocence in the form of a letter Dunya had been forced to write to him before Marfa Petrovna caught them in the garden. In this letter, which Mr. Svidrigailov had kept after Dunya left, she firmly refused all private meetings and personal explanations he had been begging for, and she reproached him with great passion for the vileness of his behavior toward Marfa Petrovna, reminding him that he was a father and head of a family, and telling him how despicable it was to torment a defenseless girl who was already unhappy enough. The letter, dear Rodya, was written so nobly and movingly that I wept as I read it and cannot read it to this day without tears. Furthermore, the testimony of the servants also cleared Dunya's name -- they had seen and known far more than Mr. Svidrigailov had supposed, as is always the case with servants. Marfa Petrovna was completely stunned, 'crushed again,' as she told us herself. But she was entirely convinced of Dunya's innocence. The very next day, a Sunday, she went straight to the cathedral, knelt down, and prayed with tears for the strength to bear this new trial and to do her duty. Then she came directly from the cathedral to us, told us the whole story, wept bitterly, and in full repentance embraced Dunya and begged her forgiveness. That same morning, without any delay, she went around to every house in town, and everywhere, shedding tears, she declared in the most flattering terms Dunya's innocence and the nobility of her feelings and conduct. She even showed and read aloud to everyone the letter Dunya had written to Mr. Svidrigailov, and allowed people to make copies of it -- which I must say strikes me as excessive. She spent several days this way, driving around the whole town, because some people had taken offense at not being visited first, so everyone had to take turns. In every house she was expected before she arrived, and people gathered for each reading, even those who had already heard it multiple times in their own homes and others'. A great deal of this was unnecessary, in my opinion, but that is Marfa Petrovna's character. In any case, she succeeded in completely restoring Dunya's reputation, and all the shame of the affair fell squarely on her husband as the sole guilty party -- so much so that I actually began to feel sorry for him. The poor madman was treated rather harshly. Dunya was immediately asked to give lessons in several families but refused. All at once, everyone started treating her with marked respect. All of this helped bring about the event that has, one might say, transformed our entire fortunes. You must know, dear Rodya, that Dunya has a suitor and has already agreed to marry him. I'm hurrying to tell you everything about it, and though it was arranged without your consent, I don't think you'll hold it against me or your sister -- you'll see that we couldn't wait to hear from you first. And you couldn't have judged the situation properly without being here. This is how it happened. He already holds the rank of counselor -- Pyotr Petrovich Luzhin -- and is a distant relative of Marfa Petrovna, who played an active role in arranging the match. It began with him expressing through her a desire to meet us. He was properly received, had coffee with us, and the very next day sent us a letter in which he very courteously proposed and asked for a prompt answer. He is a very busy man and in a great hurry to get to Petersburg, so every moment matters to him. Of course we were surprised at first -- it had all happened so fast and unexpectedly. We spent the whole day thinking and talking it over. He's a man of means, reliable, with two government positions and an established fortune. It's true he's forty-five, but he's fairly presentable in appearance and might still be considered attractive to women -- altogether a very respectable and proper man, though perhaps a bit gloomy and somewhat conceited. But that may just be the first impression. And please, dear Rodya, when he arrives in Petersburg shortly, don't judge him too hastily or harshly, as you tend to do, if something about him doesn't appeal to you right away. I say this even though I'm sure he'll make a good impression on you. Besides, to truly understand any person, you must be patient and careful, and avoid forming hasty opinions that are hard to correct later. From many signs, Pyotr Petrovich seems to be a thoroughly estimable man. At his first visit he told us he was a practical man but still shared, as he put it, many of the convictions of 'our most progressive generation' and opposed all prejudices. He said a good deal more -- he seems a bit conceited and likes an audience -- but this is hardly a serious fault. I understood very little of it, of course, but Dunya explained to me that though he isn't a highly educated man, he's intelligent and seems good-natured. You know your sister's character, Rodya. She's resolute, sensible, patient, and generous -- but she also has a passionate heart, as I know well. Of course there's no great love on either side, but Dunya is a smart girl with the heart of an angel, and she will make it her duty to make her husband happy, while he in turn will make her happiness his concern. We have no good reason to doubt that, though it must be admitted the whole thing was arranged rather quickly. He's also a very prudent man, and he'll surely see that his own happiness depends on making Dunya happy. As for certain shortcomings of character, certain habits, and even some differences of opinion -- inevitable in even the happiest marriages -- Dunya says she's confident in herself and sees nothing to worry about, that she can put up with a great deal so long as the relationship is honorable and straightforward. He did strike me at first as somewhat brusque, but that may simply be because he's a blunt man -- and that's probably all it is. For instance, on his second visit, after receiving Dunya's acceptance, he mentioned in conversation that even before meeting Dunya, he had decided to marry a respectable girl without a dowry, and ideally one who had experienced poverty, because, as he explained, a wife should not consider herself her husband's equal but should view him as her benefactor. I should add that he expressed it more politely than I've put it here -- I've forgotten his exact words and only remember the gist. And besides, it clearly wasn't said deliberately but slipped out in the heat of conversation, and he tried to walk it back afterward. Still, it struck me as somewhat rude, and I told Dunya so. But Dunya was annoyed and replied that 'words are not deeds,' which is of course perfectly true. Dunya didn't sleep at all the night before she decided. Thinking I was asleep, she got out of bed and paced the room all night. Finally she knelt before the icon and prayed long and fervently. In the morning she told me she had made up her mind.

old: "I mentioned already that Pyotr Petrovich is about to leave for Petersburg, where he has a great deal of business and wants to open a law office. He has spent many years handling civil and commercial cases, and just recently won an important one. He needs to be in Petersburg because he has a major case before the Senate. So, dear Rodya, he could be enormously useful to you, in every way, and Dunya and I have agreed that starting right now you could consider your career launched and your future settled. Oh, if only this comes true! It would be such a blessing that we could only see it as Providence. Dunya dreams of nothing else. We've even ventured to mention the subject to Pyotr Petrovich. He answered cautiously, saying that since he needs a secretary, it would be better to pay a salary to a relative than a stranger -- provided the person was qualified (as if there could be any doubt about you!) -- but he wondered whether your university studies would leave you time for office work. The matter was dropped for the moment, but Dunya can think of nothing else. She's been in a kind of fever these past few days and has already drawn up a whole plan for you to eventually become an associate and even a partner in Pyotr Petrovich's practice, which seems perfectly feasible since you're a law student. old: Almost from the very first line, Raskolnikov's face was wet with tears. But when he finished reading, his face was pale and contorted, and a bitter, angry, malicious smile played on his lips. He laid his head on his threadbare, dirty pillow and thought for a long time. His heart was pounding and his mind was in turmoil. Finally the cramped little yellow room -- no bigger than a cupboard, a coffin -- became unbearable. His eyes and his mind craved open space. He grabbed his hat and went out, this time without the fear of running into anyone -- he had forgotten that fear entirely. He headed toward Vasilyevsky Island, walking along Vasilyevsky Prospect as though he had some urgent business. But as usual, he didn't notice where he was going, muttering and even talking aloud to himself, startling passersby. Many of them assumed he was drunk.

old: His mother's letter had tortured him, but on the central issue he had not hesitated for a single moment, even while reading it. The question was settled, irrevocably settled in his mind: "This marriage will never happen while I'm alive, and Mr. Luzhin can go to hell!" "The whole thing is perfectly clear," he muttered to himself with a vicious smile, savoring his resolve. "No, Mother, no, Dunya -- you won't fool me! And they apologize for not asking my advice, for deciding without me! They think it's all arranged and can't be undone -- we'll see about that! A wonderful excuse: 'Pyotr Petrovich is such a busy man that even his wedding has to be rushed, practically by express mail.' No, Dunya, I see through it all. I know what you want to say to me. I know what you were thinking about when you paced all night, and what your prayers were like before the Holy Mother of Kazan in mother's bedroom. The road to Golgotha is bitter.... Hmm... so it's settled then: you've decided to marry a sensible businessman, Avdotya Romanovna, one who has a fortune (_already_ made his fortune -- so much more solid and impressive), a man with two government posts who shares the views of our most progressive generation, as mother writes, and who _seems_ to be kind, as Dunya herself notes. That _seems_ is everything! And that very Dunya is marrying him for that very '_seems_'! Splendid! Splendid!

old: "...But why did mother write to me about 'our most progressive generation'? Just as a descriptive detail, or to soften me up toward Mr. Luzhin? Oh, how clever of them! And I'd like to know something else: how open were they with each other that day and night and all this time? Was it all spoken aloud, or did they both understand they were thinking the same thing and there was no need to say it, better not to? Probably something like that. From mother's letter it's obvious: he struck her as somewhat rude, and mother in her simplicity shared her observation with Dunya. And of course Dunya was irritated and 'answered angrily.' Naturally! Who wouldn't be, when the point was perfectly clear without any naive questions, and discussing it was useless? And why does she write 'love Dunya, Rodya -- she loves you more than herself'? Is she secretly pricked by guilt over sacrificing her daughter for her son? 'You are everything to us, our only comfort, our only hope.' Oh, Mother!"

old: "Hmm... yes, that's true," he went on, chasing one feverish thought after another. "It's true that 'it takes time and care to know a person,' but there's no mystery about Mr. Luzhin. The main thing is he's 'a practical man and _seems_ kind' -- what a feat, arranging shipment of their bags and trunk! A kind man, obviously! But his _bride_ and her mother are supposed to ride in a peasant cart with a tarp over it. I know those carts -- I've ridden in one. Never mind! It's only ninety versts, and then they can 'travel quite comfortably in third class' for a thousand versts! Quite right. You have to live within your means. But what about you, Mr. Luzhin? She's your bride.... And you must realize that her mother has to borrow against her pension just to make the trip. Sure, it's a business arrangement -- a partnership with equal shares and shared expenses; meals included, but bring your own tobacco. The businessman has gotten the better of them here, too. The luggage will cost less than their fares and probably ship for free. How do neither of them see this? Or do they just not want to? And they're pleased, pleased! And to think this is just the beginning -- the real fruits are yet to come! But what really matters isn't the cheapness, isn't the stinginess -- it's the _tone_ of the whole thing. Because this will be the tone after the marriage. It's a preview. And Mother -- why should she spend so freely? What will she have left by the time she reaches Petersburg? Three silver rubles or two 'paper ones,' as _she_ says... that old woman... hmm. What does she plan to live on in Petersburg afterward? She already has reason to suspect she _won't_ be able to live with Dunya after the wedding, not even for the first few months. The good man has no doubt dropped a hint about that too, though mother would deny it: 'I shall refuse,' she says. So who is she counting on? On what's left of her hundred-and-twenty-ruble pension after Afanasy Ivanovich's debt is paid? She knits woolen shawls and embroiders cuffs, ruining her old eyes. And all her shawls add at most twenty rubles a year to her hundred and twenty -- I know that. So she's pinning all her hopes on Mr. Luzhin's generosity: 'He'll offer it himself, he'll insist.' You may wait a long time for that! That's how it always is with these Schilleresque noble souls: up to the very last moment every goose is a swan, up to the last moment they hope for the best and refuse to see anything wrong. And though they have an inkling of the truth, they won't face it until it's forced on them. The very thought makes them shudder. They push the truth away with both hands until the man they've dressed up in borrowed colors puts a fool's cap on them personally. I wonder if Mr. Luzhin has any medals. I bet he has the Order of St. Anna in his buttonhole and wears it to dinners with merchants and contractors. He'll certainly wear it at his wedding! To hell with him, enough.

old: "Well... Mother I can understand -- God bless her, that's how she is. But Dunya? Dunya, darling, as if I don't know you! You were almost twenty when I last saw you, and I understood you even then. Mother writes that 'Dunya can put up with a great deal.' I know that very well. I've known it for two and a half years, and for two and a half years I've been thinking about exactly that -- that 'Dunya can put up with a great deal.' If she could put up with Mr. Svidrigailov and everything else, she can certainly put up with a great deal. And now mother and she have decided she can also put up with Mr. Luzhin, who expounds his theory that wives rescued from destitution should be forever grateful to their husbands -- and expounds it practically on the first meeting. Granted, he 'let it slip,' though he's supposed to be a sensible man (or maybe it wasn't a slip at all -- maybe he wanted to make his position clear from the start). But Dunya -- Dunya? She sees through the man, of course, but she'll have to live with him. She'd live on black bread and water before she'd sell her soul. She wouldn't trade her moral freedom for comfort. She wouldn't trade it for all of Schleswig-Holstein, let alone Mr. Luzhin's money. No, Dunya was never that sort when I knew her, and... she's still the same, of course! Yes, there's no denying the Svidrigailovs are hard to swallow. Spending your life as a governess in the provinces for two hundred rubles a year is bitter. But I know she'd rather be a slave on a plantation or a serf under a German master than degrade her soul and her moral dignity by binding herself forever to a man she doesn't respect and has nothing in common with -- all for her own advantage. Even if Mr. Luzhin were made of pure gold or were one enormous diamond, she would never have agreed to become his legal concubine. So why is she agreeing? What's the point? What's the answer? It's obvious: for herself, for her own comfort, to save her own life -- she would never sell herself. But for someone else, she'll do it! For someone she loves, someone she adores, she'll sell herself! That's what it comes down to. For her brother, for her mother, she'll sell herself! She'll sell everything! In situations like this, 'we overcome our moral feelings when necessary' -- freedom, peace, conscience, everything gets brought to market. Let my life be ruined, as long as my loved ones are happy! More than that, we become rationalizers, we learn to be Jesuitical, and for a while we can even soothe ourselves, convince ourselves it's our duty for a good cause. That's exactly what's happening here, clear as day. Rodion Romanovich Raskolnikov is obviously the central figure in this whole business. Oh yes, she can secure his happiness, keep him at the university, make him a partner in the firm, guarantee his entire future. Maybe he'll even become a rich man someday -- prosperous, respected, perhaps even end his life as a famous man! But what about Mother? It's all about Rodya, precious Rodya, her firstborn! For such a son, who wouldn't sacrifice such a daughter! Oh, loving, biased hearts! Why stop there? For his sake we wouldn't even shrink from Sonya's fate -- Sonya, Sonya Marmeladov, the eternal victim, as long as the world exists. Have you both measured your sacrifice? Really measured it? Is it right? Can you bear it? Is it worth it? Is there any sense in it? Let me tell you, Dunya: Sonya's life is no worse than life with Mr. Luzhin. 'There can be no question of love,' mother writes. But what if there's no question of respect either? What if instead there's only revulsion, contempt, disgust -- what then? So you'll have to 'keep up appearances' too. Do you understand what that means? Do you understand that the Luzhin kind of smartness is exactly the same as Sonya's -- maybe worse, more vile, more degrading -- because in your case, Dunya, it's a bargain for luxuries, while for Sonya it's literally a matter of starvation? It has to be paid for, Dunya, this kind of smartness. And what if later it proves more than you can bear, and you regret it? The bitterness, the misery, the curses, the tears hidden from the whole world -- because you're not Marfa Petrovna! And how will Mother feel then? Even now she's uneasy, worried -- but when she sees it all clearly? And me? What exactly do you take me for? I won't accept your sacrifice, Dunya! I won't accept it, Mother! It will not happen as long as I'm alive! It will not! I refuse!"

old: His nervous shuddering had turned into a fever that left him shivering. Despite the heat, he felt cold. With a kind of desperate effort, he began staring at every object he passed, almost unconsciously, driven by some inner need for distraction. But it didn't work, and he kept sinking back into dark thoughts. Whenever he would startle and look up, he immediately forgot what he'd just been thinking and where he was going. In this way he walked all the way across Vasilyevsky Island, came out onto the Lesser Neva, crossed the bridge, and turned toward the islands. At first the greenery and freshness were soothing to his exhausted eyes after the dust of the city and the massive buildings that crowded in on him and weighed him down. There were no taverns here, no suffocating closeness, no stench. But soon even these pleasant new sensations turned into a morbid irritability. Sometimes he stopped in front of a brightly painted summer villa set among green foliage. He would gaze through the fence at elegantly dressed women on verandas and balconies, at children running in the gardens. The flowers especially caught his attention -- he stared at them longer than at anything. He also passed luxurious carriages and men and women on horseback. He watched them with curious eyes but forgot about them before they were out of sight. At one point he stopped and counted his money. He had thirty kopecks. "Twenty to the policeman, three to Nastasya for the letter, so I must have given forty-seven or fifty to the Marmeladovs yesterday," he calculated, for no particular reason, but soon forgot why he had taken the money out at all. He remembered when he passed a tavern, and realized he was hungry.... He went in, drank a glass of vodka, and ate some kind of pie, finishing it as he walked. It had been a long time since he'd had vodka, and it hit him immediately, even though he'd only had one small glass. His legs suddenly grew heavy and a powerful drowsiness came over him. He headed home, but when he reached Petrovsky Island, he stopped, completely spent, turned off the road into the bushes, sank down on the grass, and fell asleep instantly.

old: But Raskolnikov had grown superstitious lately. The traces of superstition lingered in him long afterward and were nearly impossible to shake. In everything that happened, he was always inclined to see something strange and mysterious, as if there were some peculiar force at work, some pattern of meaningful coincidences. The previous winter, a student he knew named Pokorev, who was leaving for Kharkov, had happened to mention in conversation the address of Alyona Ivanovna, the old pawnbroker, in case Raskolnikov ever needed to pawn something. For a long time he didn't go. He had tutoring work and was getting by. Six weeks ago he had remembered the address. He had two things he could pawn: his father's old silver watch and a little gold ring with three red stones, a farewell gift from his sister. He decided to take the ring. From the moment he first laid eyes on the old woman, he felt an overwhelming revulsion for her, though he knew nothing particular about her. He got two rubles from her and stopped at a miserable little tavern on his way home. He ordered tea, sat down, and sank into deep thought. A strange idea was pecking at his brain like a chick in an egg, and it absorbed him completely.

old: Whenever he had imagined all this beforehand, he had sometimes thought he would be very afraid. But he wasn't very afraid now -- not afraid at all, in fact. His mind was occupied with irrelevant things, though nothing for long. Passing the Yusupov Garden, he found himself absorbed in the idea of building great fountains and how they would cool the air in all the city squares. Gradually he became convinced that if the Summer Garden were extended to the Field of Mars and perhaps connected to the Mikhailovsky Palace garden, it would be a splendid thing, a great benefit to the city. Then he got interested in the question of why, in all great cities, people are not simply forced by necessity but seem somehow peculiarly drawn to live in exactly those parts of town where there are no gardens, no fountains -- where there is the most filth and stench and every kind of squalor. He'll stretch the two and a half sheets to six, we'll slap on a gorgeous half-page title, and sell it for fifty kopecks. It'll go! He pays me six rubles a sheet, which comes to about fifteen for the whole thing, and I've already had six in advance. When we finish this, we're starting on a translation about whales, and then some of the most tedious gossip from Part Two of the _Confessions_ -- we've already marked the passages. old: He could never have imagined such brutality, such frenzy. He sat up in bed in terror, nearly fainting from anguish. But the fighting, wailing, and cursing grew louder and louder. Then, to his intense amazement, he recognized his landlady's voice. She was howling, shrieking, and wailing -- rapidly, frantically, incoherently -- so that he couldn't make out what she was saying. She was begging, clearly -- begging not to be beaten, for she was being beaten mercilessly on the stairs. Her attacker's voice was so horrible with spite and rage that it was more of a rasp than a voice, but he too was saying something, just as fast and unintelligibly, rushing and sputtering. Suddenly Raskolnikov began to tremble. He recognized the voice -- it was Ilya Petrovich's. Ilya Petrovich was here, beating the landlady! He was kicking her, slamming her head against the steps -- that was clear from the sounds, the cries, the thuds. How could this be? Had the world turned upside down? He could hear people running from every floor and every staircase -- voices, exclamations, knocking, doors slamming. "But why, why -- how is this possible?" he kept repeating, seriously thinking he had gone mad. But no, he could hear it all too clearly! And then they would come for him next. "Because obviously... it's all about _that_... about yesterday.... My God!" He wanted to bolt his door, but he couldn't lift his arm... and besides, it would be pointless. Terror gripped his heart like ice, tortured him, numbed him.... But finally, after about ten minutes, the uproar gradually began to subside. The landlady moaned and groaned; Ilya Petrovich still made threats and cursed.... But at last he too seemed to fall silent, and then he was gone. "Has he really left? Dear God!" Yes, and now the landlady was leaving too, still weeping and moaning... then her door slammed.... The crowd was dispersing from the stairs back to their rooms -- exclaiming, arguing, calling to one another, their voices rising to shouts, dropping to whispers. There must have been a great many of them -- practically everyone in the building. "But, God, how can this be? And why -- why had he come here?"

old: "Oh, yes! Here is the story. Early on the third day after the murder, while they were still fussing over Koch and Pestryakov -- though those two had accounted for every step and it was plain as day -- an unexpected fact turned up. A man named Dushkin, who runs a tavern across from the building, brought a jeweler's case containing some gold earrings to the police station and told a long story. 'The day before yesterday, just after eight o'clock' -- mark the day and hour! -- 'a journeyman house painter named Nikolay, who had already been in to see me that day, brought me this case of gold earrings and stones and asked me to give him two rubles for them. When I asked where he got them, he said he picked them up in the street. I did not ask any more questions.' I am telling you Dushkin's story. 'I gave him a one-ruble note, figuring if he did not pawn them with me he would with someone else. It would all end the same way -- he would drink it up, so the goods might as well stay with me. Hide something far away and you will find it close to hand. And if any rumors come up, I will take them to the police.' Of course, that is all nonsense. He lies through his teeth. I know this Dushkin -- he is a pawnbroker and a fence, and he did not cheat Nikolay out of a thirty-ruble trinket just to hand it to the police. He was simply scared. But never mind. Back to Dushkin's story: 'I have known this Nikolay Dementyev since he was a child. He comes from the same province and district of Zaraisk -- we are both Ryazan men. And though Nikolay is not a drunkard, he does drink. I knew he had a job in that building, painting work with Dmitri, who comes from the same village too. As soon as he got the ruble, he changed it, had a couple of glasses, took his change, and left. But I did not see Dmitri with him. The next day I heard that someone had murdered Alyona Ivanovna and her sister Lizaveta Ivanovna with an axe. I knew them, and I got suspicious about the earrings right away -- I knew the murdered woman lent money on pledges. I went to the building and started making quiet inquiries. First I asked: Is Nikolay here? Dmitri told me Nikolay had gone off on a bender -- came home at dawn, drunk, stayed about ten minutes, and left again. Dmitri had not seen him since and was finishing the job alone. Their job was on the same staircase as the murder, on the second floor. When I heard all that, I said nothing to anyone, but I found out what I could about the murder and went home still suspicious. And at eight this morning' -- that was the third day, you understand -- 'I saw Nikolay come in, not sober, though not exactly very drunk -- he could understand what was said to him. He sat down on the bench and did not speak. There was only one stranger in the bar and a man I knew asleep on a bench, and my two boys. Have you seen Dmitri? I asked. No, I have not, he said. And you have not been here either? Not since the day before yesterday, he said. Where did you sleep last night? In Peski, with the Kolomensky men. And where did you get those earrings? I found them in the street -- and the way he said it was odd. He did not look at me. Did you hear what happened that very evening, at that very hour, on that very staircase? I asked. No, he said, I had not heard -- and the whole time he was listening, his eyes were bulging and he turned white as chalk. I told him everything, and he grabbed his hat and started to get up. Wait, Nikolay, I said, will you not have a drink? And I signaled the boy to block the door, and I came out from behind the bar. But he bolted out and down the street and around the corner at a run. I have not seen him since. That settled my doubts -- it was him, clear as day....'"

old: "That wasn't quite my argument," he began simply and modestly. "Still, I admit you've stated it almost correctly—perhaps perfectly so." He almost enjoyed admitting this. "The only difference is that I don't claim extraordinary people are always obliged to commit crimes, as you put it. I doubt such an argument could even be published. I simply suggested that an 'extraordinary' person has the right—not an official right but an inner right—to decide in his own conscience to overstep certain obstacles, and only when it's essential for the practical fulfillment of his idea, which may sometimes benefit all of humanity. You say my article is unclear; I'm prepared to make it as clear as I can. Perhaps I'm right in thinking you want me to—very well. I maintain that if the discoveries of Kepler and Newton could not have been made known without sacrificing the lives of one, a dozen, a hundred, or more people, Newton would have had the right—would indeed have been duty-bound—to eliminate that dozen or hundred for the sake of making his discoveries known to all humanity. But it doesn't follow that Newton had a right to murder people randomly or steal at the market every day. old: Sonia said nothing. Raskolnikov pressed her hand and left. He felt utterly wretched. If he could have escaped to some wilderness, he would have considered himself lucky — even if it meant spending his whole life there. But although he had been almost entirely alone lately, he had never managed to feel truly alone. Sometimes he would walk out of the city onto the highway; once he even reached a small woods. But the lonelier the place, the more aware he became of some uneasy presence nearby. It didn't frighten him, but it annoyed him intensely, so he would hurry back to the city, lose himself in the crowds, duck into restaurants and taverns, walk through the busiest streets. There he felt easier and, paradoxically, more solitary. One evening at dusk he sat for an hour in a tavern listening to songs, and he remembered that he actually enjoyed it. But suddenly the same unease returned, as though his conscience were pricking him. "Here I sit listening to songs — is that what I ought to be doing?" he thought. Yet he immediately sensed that wasn't the only cause; there was something demanding an immediate decision, but he couldn't put it into words or even think it through clearly. It was a hopeless tangle. "No — better to fight again! Better Porfiry again... or Svidrigailov... Better some challenge, some attack. Yes, yes!" he thought. He left the tavern and practically broke into a run. The thought of Dunya and his mother suddenly filled him with something close to panic. That night he woke before dawn among some bushes on Krestovsky Island, shivering with fever. He walked home; it was early morning when he arrived. After a few hours' sleep the fever passed, but he woke up late — two in the afternoon.

old: "Yes, it was. I can see you're extremely curious about all this, and I'll consider it my duty to satisfy your curiosity at the first opportunity. My God — I see I really could pass for a romantic figure with some people. Judge how grateful I must be to Marfa Petrovna for telling Avdotya Romanovna all that mysterious, interesting gossip about me. I can only guess what impression it made, but in any case it worked in my favor. Despite Avdotya Romanovna's natural aversion, and despite my invariably dark and repellent manner — she did come to pity me, pity a lost soul. And once a girl's heart is moved to pity, it's more dangerous than anything. She's bound to want to 'save him,' to bring him to his senses, lift him up, redirect him to nobler aims, restore him to new life and usefulness — well, we all know how far such dreams can go. I saw at once that the bird was flying into the cage on its own. And I prepared accordingly. You're frowning, Rodion Romanovitch? No need. As you know, it all ended in nothing. (Damn, I'm drinking a lot!) You know, I always regretted, from the very beginning, that fate didn't arrange for your sister to be born in the second or third century A.D. as the daughter of a reigning prince or some governor in Asia Minor. She would undoubtedly have been one of those who endured martyrdom with a smile as hot pincers seared her breast. She would have gone to it willingly. And in the fourth or fifth century, she'd have walked off into the Egyptian desert to live for thirty years on roots and ecstasies and visions. She's simply burning to endure some torment for someone, and if she can't find her torment, she'll throw herself out a window. I've heard something about a Mr. Razumikhin — they say he's a sensible fellow; his surname suggests it. He's probably a theology student. Well, he'd better look after your sister! I like to think I understand her, and I'm proud of it. But at the beginning of an acquaintance, as you know, one tends to be more careless and stupid. You don't see clearly. Damn it all — why is she so beautiful? It's not my fault. In short, it began on my side with an irresistible physical desire. Avdotya Romanovna is extraordinarily chaste — incredibly, phenomenally so. Take note: I'm telling you this about your sister as a fact. She is almost morbidly chaste, despite her broad intelligence, and it will stand in her way. There was a girl in the house then, Parasha, a dark-eyed wench I'd never seen before — she'd just arrived from another village — very pretty but incredibly stupid. She burst into tears, wailed so loudly the whole house could hear, and caused a scandal. One day after dinner, Avdotya Romanovna followed me into a garden path and, with blazing eyes, insisted I leave poor Parasha alone. It was nearly our first private conversation. I was naturally delighted to comply, tried to appear flustered and embarrassed — played my part rather well, in short. Then came more meetings, private talks, pleas, entreaties, even tears — would you believe it, even tears? Think what the passion for moral reform can bring some young women to! I, of course, blamed everything on destiny, posed as a man hungering and thirsting for enlightenment, and finally deployed the most powerful weapon for the conquest of a woman's heart — one that never fails. It's the well-known technique: flattery. Nothing in the world is harder than speaking the truth, and nothing easier than flattery. If there's even the slightest false note in speaking the truth, it creates discord, and discord means trouble. But if flattery is false from first note to last, it's still perfectly agreeable, and heard with genuine pleasure. However crude the flattery, at least half of it will seem true. That holds for all levels of education and all classes of society. Even a vestal virgin could be seduced by flattery. I can never think without laughing of how I once seduced a lady devoted to her husband, her children, and her principles. What fun it was, and how little effort! And the lady really did have principles — of her own sort, anyway. My entire strategy consisted of appearing utterly demolished and prostrate before her purity. I flattered her shamelessly, and each time I managed to get a squeeze of the hand or a glance, I'd reproach myself for having stolen it by force, declaring she'd resisted and that I could never have gotten anywhere if I weren't so shameless. I insisted she was so innocent she couldn't have foreseen my treachery, and had yielded unconsciously, without realizing it. In a word, I triumphed, while the lady remained firmly convinced she was innocent, chaste, faithful to all her duties, and had fallen purely by accident. And how angry she was when I finally told her it was my sincere belief she'd been just as eager as I! Poor Marfa Petrovna was terribly susceptible to flattery too; if I'd wanted to, I could have had all her property signed over to me during her lifetime. (I'm drinking far too much wine and talking too much.) I hope you won't be angry if I mention that I was beginning to produce the same effect on Avdotya Romanovna. But I was stupid and impatient and ruined everything. Several times — one time in particular — Avdotya Romanovna was deeply displeased by the expression of my eyes. Would you believe it? There was sometimes a light in them that frightened her, growing stronger and more brazen until it became hateful to her. No need for details, but we parted. Then I did something stupid again. I began mocking all such reforming efforts and attempts to convert me in the crudest way; Parasha returned to the scene, and not just her — in short, there was a huge uproar. Ah, Rodion Romanovitch, if you could only see how your sister's eyes can flash sometimes! Never mind that I'm drunk and have had a whole glass of wine — I'm telling you the truth. I assure you, that look haunted my dreams; eventually even the rustle of her dress became more than I could stand. I honestly began to think I might become epileptic. I would never have believed I could be driven to such frenzy. A reconciliation was essential, but by then it was impossible. And imagine what I did! To what depths of stupidity frenzy can drive a man! Never attempt anything in a frenzy, Rodion Romanovitch. I calculated that Avdotya Romanovna was, after all, a pauper (forgive me — that's not the right word, but does it matter if it conveys the meaning?), that she lived by her work, that she had her mother and you to support (you're scowling again), and I decided to offer her all my money — thirty thousand rubles I could have raised at the time — if she'd run away with me to Petersburg. Of course I'd have sworn eternal love, rapture, and the rest. And you know, I was so wild about her that if she'd told me to poison Marfa Petrovna or slit her throat and then marry me — I'd have done it at once! But it ended in the disaster you already know about. You can imagine my fury when I learned Marfa Petrovna had gotten hold of that vile attorney Luzhin and practically arranged a match — which amounted to exactly the same thing I was proposing. Am I right? Am I? I notice you've begun listening very closely... interesting young man..."

old: "I'm very fond of children — always have been," Svidrigailov laughed. "I can tell you a curious example. My first day here, I visited various haunts — after seven years, I simply threw myself at them. You've probably noticed I'm in no rush to reconnect with old friends. I'll manage without them as long as I can. You know, when I was with Marfa Petrovna in the country, the thought of these places, where a man who knows his way around can find plenty, haunted me. Yes, upon my soul! The peasants have vodka, the educated young people shut out from activity waste themselves on impossible dreams and theories; Jews spring up and hoard money; everyone else gives themselves over to debauchery. From the first hour, the city reeked of its familiar smells. I happened into a ghastly den — I like my dens filthy — and there was a so-called dance, with a cancan the likes of which I'd never seen in my day. Yes, there's progress for you. Suddenly I noticed a girl of thirteen, nicely dressed, dancing with a specialist in that line, facing another partner. Her mother was sitting in a chair by the wall. You can't imagine what that cancan was like! The girl felt ashamed, blushed, and finally felt insulted and began to cry. Her partner grabbed her, started spinning her around and performing in front of her; everyone laughed — I like your public, even the cancan public — they laughed and shouted: 'Serves her right! That's what she gets for bringing children!' Well, it's not my concern whether that reasoning was logical or not. I immediately made my plan. I sat down beside the mother and explained that I too was a stranger, that people here were rude and couldn't recognize decent folk or treat them respectfully. I let her understand I had plenty of money, offered to take them home in my carriage. I took them home and got to know them. They were staying in a miserable little hole, having just arrived from the country. She told me she and her daughter could only regard my acquaintance as an honor. I learned they had nothing of their own and had come to the city on some legal matter. I offered my services and money. I found out they'd gone to the dance hall by mistake, thinking it was a real dance school. I offered to help with the girl's education in French and dancing. The offer was accepted with enthusiasm as a great honor — and we're still on friendly terms... If you'd like, we'll go visit them — only not just now."

old: "It's for you, Sofya Semyonovna — for you. And please don't waste time arguing. I haven't got time for it. You'll need it. Rodion Romanovitch has two choices: a bullet in the brain, or Siberia." You gave him good advice when you told him to turn himself in and confess. It would be far better for him. Well, if it turns out to be Siberia, he'll go — and you'll follow him. That's how it is, isn't it? And if so, you'll need money. You'll need it for him — do you understand? Giving it to you is the same as giving it to him. Besides, you promised Amalia Ivanovna you'd pay what's owed. I heard you. How can you take on such obligations so carelessly, Sofya Semyonovna? It was Katerina Ivanovna's debt, not yours — you should have ignored the German woman. You can't get through the world that way. old: It emerged later that the same evening, just after eleven-twenty, he made another very eccentric and unexpected visit. The rain was still coming down. Drenched to the skin, he appeared at the tiny apartment where his fiancée's parents lived, on Third Street in Vasilievsky Island. He had to knock for some time before he was let in, and his visit initially caused great consternation. But Svidrigailov could be very charming when he chose, and the parents' first, quite sensible assumption — that Svidrigailov had drunk so much he didn't know what he was doing — vanished almost immediately. The decrepit father was wheeled in by the tender, sensible mother, who as usual launched the conversation with various roundabout questions. She never asked anything directly: she would begin by smiling and rubbing her hands, then, when she absolutely had to find something out — such as when Svidrigailov would like the wedding — she'd start with eager questions about Paris and court life, only gradually working her way to Third Street. On other occasions this had been quite impressive, but tonight Arkady Ivanovitch seemed unusually impatient and insisted on seeing his fiancée immediately, despite being told she had already gone to bed. The girl appeared, of course.

old: Svidrigailov informed her at once that urgent business required him to leave Petersburg for a time, and therefore he was bringing her fifteen thousand rubles as a gift, which he'd long intended to give her before the wedding. The logical connection between this gift, his imminent departure, and the absolute necessity of visiting in a downpour at midnight was never made clear. But everything went remarkably smoothly; even the inevitable exclamations of wonder and questions were unusually few and restrained. On the other hand, the gratitude expressed was most effusive, reinforced by tears from the most sensible of mothers. Svidrigailov got up, laughed, kissed his fiancée, patted her cheek, declared he'd return soon, and noticing in her eyes — alongside childish curiosity — a kind of earnest, silent question, he paused and kissed her again, though he felt genuine irritation at the thought that his gift would be immediately locked away by the most sensible of mothers. He left them all in a state of extraordinary excitement, but the tender mama, speaking quietly in a half-whisper, resolved most of their doubts by concluding that Svidrigailov was a great man, a man of great affairs and connections and great wealth — one couldn't tell what he had in his head. He might start a journey and hand out money just as the fancy took him, so there was nothing surprising in it. It was odd that he was so wet, of course, but the English, for instance, were even more eccentric, and people of the upper classes didn't care what others said and didn't stand on ceremony. Perhaps he'd come like that on purpose, to show he wasn't afraid of anyone. Above all, not a word to anyone about it — God knew what might come of it — and the money must be locked up. It was most fortunate that Fedosya the cook hadn't left the kitchen. And above all, not a word to that old cat Madame Resslich. They sat whispering until two in the morning, but the girl went to bed much earlier, amazed and rather sorrowful.

old: Svidrigailov, meanwhile, at exactly midnight, was crossing the bridge back to the mainland. The rain had stopped and a roaring wind had risen. He began to shiver, and for one moment he stared at the black waters of the Little Neva with a look of special interest, almost inquiry. But he soon decided it was too cold standing by the water; he turned and headed toward Y— Prospect. He walked along that endless street for a long time, nearly half an hour, stumbling more than once in the dark on the wooden pavement, but constantly scanning the right side of the street for something. He'd noticed recently, passing through this area, a wooden hotel of a fair size, and its name — something like the Adrianople — had stuck in his memory. He was right: the hotel was conspicuous enough in that godforsaken place to be visible even in the dark. It was a long, blackened wooden building, and despite the late hour, lights glowed in the windows and there were signs of life inside. He went in and asked a ragged fellow in the corridor for a room. The man looked Svidrigailov up and down, pulled himself together, and led him at once to a cramped, tiny room at the far end of the corridor, under the stairs. There was nothing else — everything was taken. The ragged man looked at him expectantly.

old: Svidrigailov got up, shaded the candle with his hand, and noticed light seeping through a crack in the wall. He went over and peered through. The neighboring room, somewhat larger than his, had two occupants. One, a very curly-haired man with a red, inflamed face, stood in an orator's pose — coatless, legs spread wide for balance — thumping his own chest. He was reproaching the other man for being a beggar, for having no standing whatsoever, declaring he'd pulled him out of the gutter and could throw him back whenever he pleased, and that only Providence could see the truth of it. The object of this tirade sat in a chair looking like a man who desperately needs to sneeze but can't. He would occasionally turn sheepish, bleary eyes on the speaker but obviously had no idea what was being said and barely heard it. A candle was guttering on the table amid glasses, a nearly empty bottle of vodka, bread and cucumbers, and glasses with dregs of stale tea. After studying this scene, Svidrigailov turned away indifferently and sat back on the bed.

old: The ragged attendant returned with the tea and couldn't resist asking once more whether the gentleman wanted anything else. Receiving another negative, he withdrew for good. Svidrigailov drank a glass of tea to warm himself but couldn't eat a bite. He was beginning to feel feverish. He took off his coat, wrapped himself in the blanket, and lay down. He was annoyed. "It would have been better to be healthy for the occasion," he thought with a grim smile. The room was stuffy, the candle burned dimly, the wind howled outside, a mouse scratched in the corner, and the whole room smelled of mice and leather. He lay in a kind of half-dream: one thought chased another. He longed to fix his imagination on something. "There must be a garden under the window," he thought. "The sound of trees. How I hate the sound of trees on a stormy night in the dark! They give you a horrible feeling." He remembered disliking it when he'd passed Petrovsky Park earlier. This reminded him of the bridge over the Little Neva, and he felt cold again as he had standing there. "I've never liked water," he thought, "not even in a painting." He suddenly smiled at a strange idea: "You'd think at a time like this, all these questions of taste and comfort shouldn't matter — and yet I've become more particular, like an animal that picks a special spot for... such an occasion. I should have gone to Petrovsky Park! I suppose it seemed too dark, too cold — ha-ha! As if I needed pleasant sensations!... By the way, why haven't I blown out the candle?" He blew it out. "They've gone to bed next door," he thought, seeing no light through the crack. "Well then, Marfa Petrovna — now would be the time for you to appear. It's dark, and the place couldn't be more fitting. But of course, now you won't come!"

old: He sat up on the edge of the bed with his back to the window. "Better not to sleep at all," he decided. A cold, damp draft seeped from the window. Without getting up, he pulled the blanket over himself and wrapped it tight. He wasn't thinking about anything and didn't want to think. But images rose one after another, incoherent scraps of thought without beginning or end drifted through his mind. He began sinking into drowsiness. Perhaps the cold, or the damp, or the darkness, or the wind howling outside and shaking the trees stirred a persistent craving for the fantastical. He kept dwelling on flowers. He imagined a lovely flower garden, a bright, warm, almost hot day — a holiday, Trinity Sunday. A fine, lavish country house in the English style, overgrown with fragrant flowers, with flower beds running all around it. The porch, twined with climbing plants, was surrounded by beds of roses. A light, cool staircase carpeted with rich rugs was adorned with rare plants in porcelain pots. He noticed especially, in the windows, bouquets of tender white narcissus, heavily fragrant, drooping over their bright green, thick long stems. He was reluctant to move away from them, but he went up the stairs and entered a large, tall drawing room — and again, everywhere, at the windows, by the doors onto the balcony, on the balcony itself — flowers. The floors were strewn with freshly cut, fragrant hay; the windows were open; a fresh, cool, light breeze drifted into the room. Birds chirped outside the window. In the middle of the room, on a table draped in a white satin shroud, stood a coffin. The coffin was covered in white silk with a thick white frill; wreaths of flowers surrounded it on all sides. Among the flowers lay a girl in a white muslin dress, arms crossed and pressed to her breast, as if carved from marble. But her loose fair hair was wet; a wreath of roses circled her head. old: Svidrigailov came to himself, rose from the bed, and went to the window. He found the latch and opened it. The wind lashed into the tiny room, stinging his face and chest through his shirt with an icy bite. Under the window there must have been something like a garden — a pleasure garden, apparently. There, too, tea-tables probably stood and songs were sung during the day. Now rain flew in from the trees and bushes; it was as dark as a cellar, and he could barely make out a few dim shapes. Svidrigailov leaned on the windowsill with both elbows and stared into the darkness for five minutes. The boom of a cannon, then another, sounded through the dark night. "The flood signal! The river is rising," he thought. "By morning, the water will be swirling through the streets in the low-lying parts, flooding the basements and cellars. old: He walked for some time through a long, narrow corridor without finding anyone and was about to call out when suddenly, in a dark corner between an old cupboard and the doorframe, he noticed a strange object that seemed to be alive. He bent down with the candle and saw a little girl — no more than five years old — shivering and crying, her clothes as wet as a sopping dishrag. She didn't seem afraid of Svidrigailov but stared at him with blank amazement from her big dark eyes. Now and then she sobbed, the way children do when they've been crying a long time but are beginning to calm down. The child's face was pale and exhausted; she was numb with cold. "How could she have gotten here? She must have hidden and never slept." He began questioning her. The child suddenly came to life, chattering in her baby language about "mommy" and how "mommy would hit her" and about some cup she'd "bwoken." She prattled on without stopping. He could only piece together from her words that she was a neglected child whose mother — probably a drunken cook employed at the hotel — beat and terrorized her. The girl had broken one of her mother's cups and was so frightened that she'd run away the evening before, hidden outside in the rain for ages, finally crept inside, hidden behind the cupboard, and spent the whole night there, crying and shivering in the damp, the dark, and the terror of being beaten. He picked her up, carried her to his room, set her on the bed, and began undressing her. Her torn shoes, on stockingless feet, were as wet as if they'd been standing in a puddle all night. When he'd undressed her, he put her in the bed, covered her up, and wrapped her in the blanket from head to toe. She fell asleep instantly. Then he sank back into gloomy brooding.

old: "What a fool I am, getting involved," he thought with a sudden feeling of oppressive annoyance. "What idiocy!" In his vexation he picked up the candle, intending to find the ragged attendant and leave at once. "Damn the child!" he thought, reaching for the door — but he turned back to check whether she was sleeping. He carefully lifted the blanket. The child was sleeping soundly and had gotten warm. Her pale cheeks had flushed. But the flush seemed brighter and coarser than a normal rosy glow of childhood. "It's a fever flush," Svidrigailov thought. It looked more like the flush from alcohol — as though she'd been given a full glass of wine. Her crimson lips were hot and burning. But what was this? He suddenly thought her long dark lashes were quivering, as though the lids were lifting and a sly, crafty eye was peeping out with an unchildlike wink — as if the little girl weren't asleep at all but pretending. Yes — that was it. Her lips parted in a smile. The corners of her mouth quivered, as though she were trying to hold it back. But now she gave up all pretense. It was a grin — a broad grin. There was something shameless, provocative in that utterly unchildlike face; it was corruption, the face of a prostitute, the brazen face of a French harlot. Now both eyes were open wide, turning a glowing, shameless stare on him; they laughed, they invited... There was something infinitely hideous and revolting in that laugh, in those eyes, in such depravity in the face of a child. "What? At five years old?" Svidrigailov whispered in genuine horror. "What does this mean?" And now she turned to him, her little face all aglow, reaching out her arms... "Accursed child!" Svidrigailov cried, raising his hand to strike her — but at that moment he woke up.

old: A thick, milky fog lay over the city. Svidrigailov walked along the slippery, dirty wooden pavement toward the Little Neva. He was picturing the waters of the Little Neva, swollen in the night — Petrovsky Island, the wet paths, the wet grass, the wet trees and bushes — and finally, that bush... He began irritably staring at the buildings, trying to think of something else. Not a cab or a soul in the street. The bright yellow little wooden houses looked dirty and dejected with their shutters closed. The cold and damp penetrated his whole body, and he started shivering. Now and then he passed a shop sign and read each one carefully. At last he reached the end of the wooden pavement and came to a large stone building. A dirty, shivering dog crossed his path, tail between its legs. A man in a greatcoat lay face down across the sidewalk, dead drunk. He glanced at him and walked on. A tall tower loomed on his left.
